message.content: I am planning a small vegetable garden behind my house and I have never grown anything before. The soil is heavy clay, the yard gets about six hours of sun, and I can spend one hour each evening on the work. Where should I start, and what should I plant first so that I do not get discouraged?

Start with the soil, because clay is the main problem. Clay holds water and then turns hard, so roots struggle to spread. Mix a thick layer of compost into the top fifteen centimeters, and do not dig when the ground is wet, since wet clay forms clumps that last all season. A raised bed about one meter wide and two meters long is a good first size. You can reach the middle from both sides, and you never need to step on the soil.

For the first season, choose plants that forgive mistakes. Radishes sprout in days and are ready in about a month, so you see a result quickly. Lettuce and spinach like cool weather and grow well in partial shade. Bush beans fix some of their own nitrogen and give a steady harvest. Zucchini needs more room but rewards you with more fruit than you can eat. Water deeply twice each week instead of a little every day, because deep watering pushes roots downward.
That helps a lot. How do I deal with slugs and with the weeds that will certainly arrive?

Mulch is your best tool against weeds. Spread five centimeters of straw or shredded leaves over the bare soil once the seedlings are tall enough to stand on their own. It blocks light, keeps moisture in the ground, and breaks down into food for the next year. Pull the weeds that still appear when they are small, ideally after a rain. For slugs, go out at dusk with a flashlight and remove them by hand for a week or two, then place a shallow dish of beer near the bed. Keep a notebook of what you plant and when, because next year it will save you from guessing.
